Thunderstorms over the greater Phoenix metropolitan area produced locally heavy rainfall during the evening hours on August 3rd. A trained weather spotter near Cave Creek Road and Union Hills reported one half inch of rain within 20 minutes. The heavy rainfall produced curb to curb street flooding. Another spotter 5 miles northwest of Paradise Valley reported 0.41 inches of rainfall within 10 minutes.

Strong thunderstorms affected the community of San Carlos during the late afternoon hours on August 12th. Damaging microburst winds were produced by the storms. According to local law enforcement personnel, gusty winds estimated to be around 60 knots blew down numerous power poles in and around San Carlos. In addition, the strong winds blew down a number of trees in the community.

Strong thunderstorms in the community of San Carlos produced locally heavy rainfall during the late afternoon and early evening hours on August 12th. Radar estimated that between 2 and 3 inches of rain fell across San Carlos, and according to local law enforcement personnel the rainfall led to flooding of streets across the community. Additionally, the heavy rain caused area washes to run heavily.

Strong thunderstorms moved across the greater Phoenix metropolitan area during the early evening hours of August 18th. According to local broadcast media sources, a wind gust measured at 62 mph occurred at Zuni Hills elementary school, located about 3 miles northwest of Sun City. No damage was reported at the school.

Thunderstorms with damaging microburst winds affected the San Tan Valley area during the afternoon hours on August 18th. A trained National Weather Service storm spotter 4 miles west of Magma reported that 1 foot diameter trees were blown down. Additionally, a roof was blown off of a house. Wind speeds were estimated to be at least 60 mph. Hail one quarter inch in diameter occurred in association with the strong storms.

Thunderstorms with damaging microburst winds affected the area around Magma during the afternoon hours on August 18th. According to a report from the local utility company, approximately 30 power poles were blown down in the Johnson Ranch area, along the Hunt highway near Judd road. Winds were estimated to be in excess of 50 knots.

Strong thunderstorms with damaging microburst winds moved through the San Tan Valley during the late afternoon hours on August 18th. Area law enforcement personnel reported that power lines were down at Bella Vista and Gantzel roads, and at least one of the lines fell onto a school bus from the Florence Unified school district. The bus driver and four children that were aboard were not injured.

Thunderstorms with strong gusty winds developed over the southeastern portion of the greater Phoenix area during the afternoon hours of August 18th. A trained weather spotter approximately 5 miles east of Sun Lakes estimated a peak wind gust to 60 mph. The strong winds were associated with a dust storm moving through the area; at the same time visibility had lowered to less than one quarter of a mile.

Strong thunderstorms developed over the south central deserts during the late afternoon hours on August 18th. The strong outflow winds from the storms generated a dust storm which moved steadily from the southeastern valley towards the northwest from approximately 5 pm through 8 pm. Much of the greater Phoenix area was affected. A number of trained weather spotters reported visiblities down to one quarter of a mile or below in dense blowing dust. A weather spotter 5 miles east of Sun Lakes reported visibility below one quarter of a mile in blowing dust at 520 pm. At 523 pm the official weather station at Mesa Gateway airport measured a visibility of one quarter mile.

Thunderstorms with locally heavy rainfall developed in the area around Magma during the late afternoon hours on August 18th. Rainfall, with rates estimated in excess of one inch per hour, led to flash flooding on the Hunt Highway west of Magma. The flooding was reported by an amateur radio operator.

Strong high pressure and a dry airmass led to excessive heat over the lower deserts of Arizona, starting Monday August 22nd and continuing through the end of the month. The hottest days during the heat wave were the first five, Monday through Friday, when the highs at Phoenix ranged from 113 to 117 degrees. The five consecutive days at or above 113 ties for the third longest streak of days with a high of 113 or greater. The 117 degree maximum on Friday August 26 not only broke the record for the date, but was the latest 117 degree maximum ever recorded, and the highest temperature ever recorded for the month of August. The extreme head led to the deaths of two people in the Phoenix area. A 70 year old woman was found dead Wednesday morning in her Surprise home after her air conditioner failed and the temperature rose to 107 degrees. Surprise Fire Captain Renee Hambin indicated that the cause of death was obviously related to the excessive heat inside her home. Additionally, a 75 year old Glendale man was found dead in his home on Thursday August 25th. Police went to his home as part of a welfare check and found him dead with the air conditioner blowing hot air and the temperature in excess of 100 degrees. Police Sgt. Brent Coombs said that the heat was definitely a factor in the man's death.

Strong high pressure developed over southeast California during late August, and led to excessive heat across Joshua Tree National Park beginning on Monday August 22nd. High temperatures across the east end of the park climbed well in excess of 100 degrees Monday, and peaked above 110 Tuesday through Saturday. The excessive heat led to the deaths of a 44 year old Dutch man and a 38 year old German woman on Monday afternoon. According to Lt. Tingle of the Sheriff's Indio station, the bodies were found near Black Eagle Mine road. The dead man was found on the edge of the road, about a mile and a half east of Pinto Basin Road, north of the Cottonwood Visitor's Center. The dead woman was found about one mile east of the man's body. Captain Raymond Gregory of the Sheriff's Indio station reported that the pair entered the park shortly before noon, and that they abandoned their vehicle in an area deemed impassable to passenger vehicles. Evidence indicated that they both succumbed to exposure to the elements.

Scattered thunderstorms developed in the Yuma area during the late evening hours on August 27th, and the storms generated strong and gusty winds. The official ASOS weather station in Yuma measured a peak wind gust of 50 knots at 1030 pm. The gusty winds also generated areas of dense blowing sand and dust; the Yuma observation reported visibility down to one quarter of a mile in blowing dust.

Scattered high based thunderstorms developed over southwestern Maricopa county during the evening hours on August 27th. The storms generated strong and gusty outflow winds. The Oatman RAWS weather station measured a wind gust of 62 mph at 852 pm. The wind gust did not cause any damage.

Scattered strong thunderstorms moved across portions of southwestern Arizona, including the community of Yuma, during the late evening hours on August 27th. The storms generated gusty and damaging winds, estimated to be in excess of 55 mph. A trained weather spotter one mile north of the Fortuna Foothills reported numerous awnings and shutters damaged or torn from their houses.

Scattered strong thunderstorms moved across the community of Yuma during the late evening hours on August 27th. The storms produced gusty and damaging winds estimated to be in excess of 60 mph. According to Yuma law enforcement personnel, numerous large trees and power poles were blown down across the city. No injuries were reported due to the damaging winds.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across eastern Imperial county during the late evening hours on August 27th. The storms generated strong and gusty outflow winds. The Squaw Lake RAWS weather station, located 4 miles southwest of Martinez Lake, measured a wind gust of 66 mph at approximately 1030 pm. No damage was reported in association with the strong winds.

Isolated high based thunderstorms developed in the Wickenburg area during the late afternoon hours on August 26th. The storms generated strong gusty winds, estimated by local law enforcement to be upwards of 70 mph. The strong winds downed several power poles which caused the area near North Vulture Mine Road and Easy Street to be closed to traffic.

Thunderstorms with strong, damaging winds moved through the Yuma foothills during the afternoon hours on September 5th. At 425 pm, a trained weather spotter estimated a wind gust to be 60 mph. The spotter, located a few miles west of the Fortuna Foothills, also reported that a roof was partially blown off of a shed by the high winds.

Thunderstorms with strong damaging winds moved through the Yuma area during the afternoon hours on September 5th.  A trained weather spotter located 5 miles north of the Fortuna Foothills reported that a box truck was blown over on Highway 95 just south of the Gila river. The wind gusts were estimated to be in excess of 50 knots. In addition, the strong microburst winds leveled an outbuilding.

Thunderstorms with strong gusty winds moved through the Yuma area during the afternoon hours on September 5th, and the strong winds generated significant blowing sand and dust. Local law enforcement personnel relayed widespread reports of visibilities below one quarter of a mile due to dense blowing dust, city-wide. A dust storm warning was issued for the Yuma area from 4 pm until 6 pm.

Thunderstorms with locally heavy rainfall moved slowly across the Yuma area during the afternoon hours on September 5th. The heavy rain prompted the issuance of a small stream flood advisory for portions of west central Yuma county including the city of Fortuna Foothills. A trained weather spotter in the Yuma foothills reported 4.3 inches of rainfall, however no serious flooding was reported in the area.

Scattered thunderstorms developed over the south central Arizona deserts during the evening hours on September 9th. The storms produced strong, damaging winds estimated to be at least 50 knots. According to local law enforcement, strong winds caused a number of power lines to be downed near the town of Maricopa at approximately 8 pm.

Scattered thunderstorms with strong, damaging winds developed over the south central Arizona deserts during the evening hours on September 9th. A trained weather spotter reported that shingles were torn off the roofs of several homes located about 11 miles west of Stanfield. In addition, mobile home skirting was damaged or destroyed on several of the mobile homes. A wind gust to 49 mph was measured, however peak gusts were likely in excess of 60 mph.

Strong thunderstorms developed across the eastern portion of the greater Phoenix area during the evening hours on September 10th. At approximately 6 pm, a National Weather Service employee in east Mesa estimated a thunderstorm wind gust to 70 mph. No damage was reported with this gust.

Strong thunderstorms with damaging microburst winds affected part of the eastern Phoenix metropolitan area during the evening hours on September 10th. A trained weather spotter, near Brown and Ellsworth roads in east Mesa, reported that trees were downed due to winds estimated at 70 mph.

Thunderstorms with strong gusty winds moved across eastern portions of the greater Phoenix area during the evening hours on September 10th. A trained weather spotter, located about 5 miles northeast of Paradise Valley, estimated a peak wind gust to 60 mph. No damage was reported with this wind gust.

Thunderstorms with damaging microburst winds moved across the Florence area during the evening hours on September 10th. A trained weather spotter in northeast Florence reported roof damage to several carports. Winds were estimated to be in excess of 50 knots.

Scattered thunderstorms with strong damaging winds moved across eastern portions of the greater Phoenix area during the evening hours on September 10th. According to reports from local broadcast media, 7 power poles were downed in the city of Mesa at the intersection of University Drive and 70th Street. Winds were estimated to be near 60 knots.

Scattered thunderstorms with strong damaging wind moved across the eastern greater Phoenix area during the evening hours on September 10th. At 830 pm a trained weather spotter in Chandler reported that several tree branches as large as 9 inches in diameter were broken off by strong wind. At approximately 8 pm, local media reported a number of trees down in northeast Gilbert, between Elliot and Baseline roads on Val Vista.

Strong thunderstorms moved across the eastern greater Phoenix area during the evening hours on September 10th, and some of them produced large hail. A National Weather Service employee in east Mesa reported hail estimated to be one inch in diameter. No damage was reported in association with the large hail.

Strong thunderstorms with damaging winds moved across the northeastern portions of the greater Phoenix area during the evening hours on September 10th. A trained weather spotter reported that numerous large tree branches were blown down near the intersection of Scottsdale road and Westland Road, a few miles south of Carefree. Winds were estimated to be in excess of 50 knots.

Scattered thunderstorms with strong and damaging winds moved across the eastern portions of the greater Phoenix area during the evening hours on September 10th. According to a National Weather Service storm survey in Mesa, winds estimated to be at least 60 knots downed multiple trees with diameters up to 14 inches. In addition, the winds caused shingle damage to area homes.

Strong thunderstorms developed across northwest Pinal county during the evening hours on September 10th. Gusty outflow winds from the thunderstorms generated a dust storm over portions of the county, including the corridor from Casa Grande through Maricopa. Several trained weather spotters reported visibility at or below one quarter mile in blowing dust. At 709 pm, a spotter in Casa Grande reported visibility less than 1/8 of a mile in a dust storm.

Thunderstorms with large hail moved through the Western fringes of the Phoenix metropolitan area during the afternoon hours on September 11th. A trained weather spotter at the Palo Verde fire station near Wintersburg reported hail varying from pea-sized to silver dollar sized. The largest hail reported was estimated to be nearly one and one half inch in diameter. No damage was reported associated with the large hail.

Thunderstorms with damaging microburst winds moved through the town of Maricopa during the late afternoon hours on September 11th. A trained weather spotter reported that strong thunderstorm winds, estimated to be in excess of 40 knots, blew down a segment of a brick wall. Additionally, it was reported in a local newspaper that approximately 80 trees were blown down at the El Rancho El Dorado subdivision and the Duke golf course in Maricopa. The trees varied in size with the largest being about 10 inches in diameter. Peak winds that downed the trees may have exceeded 50 knots.

Thunderstorms to the south of the greater Phoenix area produced gusty outflow winds which stirred up significant dust and generated a dust storm which moved into the central and eastern portions of the greater Phoenix area during the early evening hours on September 11th. Multiple trained weather spotters reported visibility at or below one quarter mile in dense blowing dust...including a spotter in Laveen at 7th Avenue and Interstate 10. The blowing dust was a significant hazard to motorists during the latter stages of the rush hour.

Thunderstorms produced large hail in the Yuma area during the afternoon hours on September 12th. A trained weather spotter reported hail as big as three quarters of an inch in diameter at the intersection of Avenue 6E and 32nd Street, near Araby. No damage was reported with the large hail.

Thunderstorms to the southeast of Yuma generated strong and gusty outflow winds which moved into the Yuma area and generated a significant dust storm. Several trained weather spotters reported visibility at or below one quarter of a mile in blowing dust and sand. At about 330 pm, a weather service employee 8 miles southeast of Somerton reported visibility down to 1/8 of a mile in dense blowing dust and sand. The dust storm was a significant hazard to motorists in the Yuma area during the afternoon rush hour.

Isolated strong thunderstorms developed in the Yuma area during the afternoon hours on September 12th, and they produced gusty and damaging microburst winds. According to the Park manager at 5201 E US highway 95, strong winds blew down two big trees which fell on a large building full of equipment and stored materials. This caused an estimated 30,000 dollars of damage to the building, fencing and equipment. In addition, the front sign that showed where trailers were located was damaged.

On the morning of September 11th, a 31 year old Missouri man and his friend decided to hike up South Mountain. The Missouri man was in town to watch the ASU/Missouri football game on Saturday the 10th. The two men went hiking in South Mountain Preserve Sunday morning and left with both water and a map. According to Scott Walker of the Phoenix Fire Department, they got lost and ran out of water at approximately 11 am and became disoriented. The hikers were deep in the mountains when a 12:40 pm emergency call was made. The Missouri man was found dead at 2 pm and rescuers indicated he died from heat stroke and dehydration. The second man survived and did not need hospitalization. The high temperature at Phoenix on Sunday was 99 degrees and some of the hotter deserts reached triple digits.

Strong thunderstorms moved through central Riverside county during the morning of September 13th, and they produced gusty and damaging winds in the Chiriaco Summit area. According to a COOP observer, A 60 foot tall tree with a 3 inch diameter trunk was blown down by winds estimated to be at least 60 mph. The tree fell down and demolished a fence.

Thunderstorms with strong, damaging winds moved through the Desert Center area during the morning hours on September 13th. Fire Department personnel reported that a 20 by 40 foot patio cover at the fire station was ripped by strong winds. The winds, estimated to be in excess of 50 knots, also knocked down several palm fronds. The fire station was located just to the northeast of the Desert Center airport.

Thunderstorms with damaging microburst winds moved through Imperial county during the afternoon hours on September 13th. According to the California Highway Patrol, 18 power poles were blown down along Highway 98 near Rood Road, east of Calexico. The strong winds also caused a semi-truck to roll over on Highway 98. Additionally, two semi trucks rolled over on Interstate 8 and State Route 7. The wind gusts were estimated to be at least 60 knots.

Thunderstorms with damaging microburst winds moved through Imperial county during the afternoon hours on September 13th. Law enforcement personnel reported that part of a building, an older structure, was blown onto the road near the intersection of Orchard and Bailey, in the community of Holtville. The winds were estimated to be at least 65 knots.

Thunderstorms with torrential rain developed across Joshua Tree National Park during the morning hours on September 13. Park employee estimates along with radar rainfall estimates indicated that at least 3 inches of rain fell in the park with the thunderstorms. Joe Zarki, Public Information Officer for the park, stated that extensive flood damage occurred to Park Route 11, the Pinto Basin Road, with loss of pavement in numerous areas. The Cottonwood Visitor's Center was flooded and parts of the Cottonwood Campground were washed away. No visitors or park employees were injured during the flash flooding and no vehicles were damaged.

Thunderstorms with locally heavy rainfall developed across portions of central Riverside county, from Joshua Tree National Park south to the Salton Sea. Radar estimated that at least 3 inches of rain fell in areas west of Chiriaco Summit since 6 am. The heavy rain led to flash flooding near the north side of the Salton Sea, east of Desert Beach. Law enforcement personnel reported that the flash flooding washed out a bridge on Highway 111 and Desert Beach Drive.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall across portions of central Riverside county, including the area around Desert Center, during the morning hours on September 13. Thunderstorms started in the mid morning, and trained over the same area for several hours. Radar estimated that 3 to 4 inches of rain fell with the storms, and this led to flash flooding. At around 1220 pm, Department of Highways personnel reported that water was flowing across State Route 177 between mile markers 7 and 10.

Isolated thunderstorms developed in the area near the town of Maricopa during the afternoon hours on September 13. The storms produced gusty winds estimated to be at least 50 knots. A trained weather spotter reported that the strong winds blew down power lines over several houses near the Maricopa Train Station at the intersection of Taft and McDavid roads. No injuries were reported in association with the downed power lines.

Isolated thunderstorms near El Centro generated strong and gusty outflow winds during the afternoon hours on October 3rd. The California highway patrol reported that power poles and live power lines were blown down along Bowker road near Interstate 8. The poles were blown down by the outflow winds which were estimated to be at least 60 knots.

Isolated thunderstorms developed across Imperial county during the afternoon hours on October 3rd. The storms generated gusty outflow winds estimated to be at least 50 knots. According to the California Highway Patrol, the strong winds blew down a number of large trees across the road near the intersection of Ross and Bowker roads, about 5 miles east of El Centro. The Highway Patrol did not mention the diameter of the trees that were downed.

Thunderstorms developed over the south central deserts during the early afternoon hours on October 4th. The storms produced gusty outflow winds; due to very dry conditions the winds generated dust storm conditions in the Casa Grande area. According to the Department of Highways, a major accident occurred near 240 pm, which involved eight vehicles. The accident was located at milepost 190, about 4 miles north of Casa Grande on Interstate 10. No fatalities were reported, but there were two serious, yet non life-threatening injuries. East bound lanes of Interstate 10 were closed for an hour due to the accident. Additionally, there were two other crashes later in the day which likely were the result of dust. A crash involving two tractor-trailers and a small car on Interstate 10 near the Gila River Indian Community south of Phoenix seriously injured two people.  Another crash occurred on Interstate 10 near Tonopah, but it did not involve serious injuries.

Strong gusty winds developed across the central deserts in advance of an approaching Pacific low pressure system during the afternoon hours on October 5th. Light rain and rain showers were present in the Phoenix area, and at 3 pm a peak wind gust of 61 knots was recorded at the Luke Air Force Base weather station. The gust was not associated with a thunderstorm, and the observation reported the presence of a squall.

Isolated to scattered showers developed across the central Arizona deserts during the evening hours on September 24th. No lightning was reported in the greater Phoenix area, however the very dry lower atmosphere allowed strong gusty winds to develop near the showers and associated virga. A local utility company reported that power lines were downed on Sherman Street between 19th Avenue and 23rd Avenue, and resulted in the loss of power to 1100 customers. The damaging winds were sub severe and according to radar estimates and surrounding observations ranged from 40 to 45 mph.

A cold front moved across the greater Phoenix metropolitan area during the late evening hours on November 4th. Isolated weak thunderstorms developed in association with the cold front. The combination of the frontal passage and thunderstorm downdrafts produced a measured wind gust of 61 mph at Phoenix Sky Harbor Airport. The wind gust was recorded by the official ASOS wind sensor. The time of the gust was 1111 pm.

A cold front moved east across the greater Phoenix area during the late evening hours on November 4th. Isolated weak thunderstorms developed in the vicinity of the cold front. The combination of the front and the thunderstorm downdrafts produced gusty and damaging winds. A trained weather spottered reported that strong winds blew down a tree 1/8th of a mile west of the intersection of Germann and Power roads in Gilbert. The spotter estimated the tree height at 20 feet, and the diameter at 1 foot. Peak wind gusts were estimated to be around 60 knots.

A cold front slowly moved east across the southern Arizona deserts during the day on November 4th. Strong southerly winds developed ahead of the front, and due to very dry conditions, they created periods of dense blowing dust. At times, dust storm conditions developed, mainly south and east of the greater Phoenix area. At 212 pm, the Department of Highways reported that visibilities as low as zero miles forced the closure of Interstate 8 at Bianco road, approximately 7 miles southwest of Casa Grande. Earlier at 140 pm, a trained weather spotter in Sacaton reported 1/4 mile visibility in a dust storm. Later, at 3 pm, another trained spotter 5 miles of Sun Lakes reported 1/8 mile visibility in a dust storm, with winds gusting to 35 mph.

events.cz_name: IMPERIAL COUNTY EXCEPT THE LOWER COLORADO RIVER VALLEY
events.event_narrative: Isolated thunderstorms developed across portions of Imperial county during the very early morning hours on July 3rd. The storms generated strong gusty outflow winds which led to dense blowing dust and sand in the area around Brawley. At 115 am, a trained weather spotter 3 miles southeast of Alamoria reported zero visibility in blowing dust. Winds were estimated to be between 40 and 50 mph.

Very strong thunderstorms developed southeast of the greater Phoenix area and north of Tucson during the late afternoon hours on July 5th. The storms produced gusty outflow winds in excess of 50 mph which moved to the northwest and across northwest Pinal county. The strong winds generated dense blowing dust which turned into a massive haboob more than one mile high. A number of weather spotters reported visibilities down to near zero miles, with winds between 35 and 55 mph. At 645 pm, a trained spotter near Arizona City reported zero visibility with winds gusting up to 55 mph. Another spotter in Johnson Ranch reported visibility down to 150 feet with winds 30 mph or greater. The massive haboob significantly disrupted traffic across northwest Pinal county during the early evening hours.

Strong thunderstorms formed over the south central deserts, to the southeast of the greater Phoenix area, during the late afternoon hours on July 4th. Strong gusty outflow winds in excess of 40 mph produced dense blowing dust over portions of northwest Pinal county, and prompted the issuance of a dust storm warning. At 640 pm a trained weather spotter in Arizona City reported dense dust with visibility less than one quarter mile. A few spotters in the Casa Grande area reported a dirt storm with visibilities down to 200 feet.

Intense thunderstorms developed over portions of central Pinal county during the afternoon hours on August 18th. The storms produced strong and gusty outflow winds in excess of 50 mph which moved towards the northwest and generated a significant haboob. The haboob moved from the Eloy/Casa Grande/Coolidge area towards the northwest and into the greater Phoenix metropolitan area. The haboob was at least 2000 feet high and 50 miles wide. Between 4 and 430 pm, several trained spotters in the Coolidge and Casa Grande area reported a dust storm with visibilities at or below one quarter mile. At 5 pm, zero visibility in dense blowing dust was reported along the Hunt Highway in the San Tan valley. The haboob significantly disrupted the rush hour traffic across northwest Pinal county. Fortunately no major accidents or injuries were reported.

Isolated thunderstorms developed across the south central deserts during the late afternoon hours on August 26th, and they generated strong gusty winds which led to dust storm conditions over portions of northwest Pinal county. Multiple trained spotters in the community of Casa Grande reported visibilities at or below one quarter mile in dense blowing dust. One of the spotters in Casa Grande reported 50 foot visibility in a dust storm. The sharply reduced visibility was a major disruption to area motorists during the rush hour.

Isolated thunderstorms developed across the south central deserts during the late afternoon hours on August 26th, and they generated strong gusty winds which led to dust storm conditions over portions of the greater Phoenix area. A few trained spotters across the greater Phoenix area reported visibilities at or below one quarter mile in dense blowing dust. A spotter in Avondale reported zero visibility in blowing dust. The sharply reduced visibility was a major disruption to area motorists during the rush hour. Fortunately, no major accidents or injuries were reported with this dust storm.

A cold and slow moving Pacific low pressure system moved across Arizona during the weekend of December 3rd and 4th, and it brought locally heavy snowfall to the higher terrain of south central Arizona. The majority of heavy snow fell from the afternoon of December 3rd through the early morning hours on Sunday December 4th. According to law enforcement personnel, 3 to 4 inches of snow fell in Globe from Saturday afternoon through about 5 am Sunday morning. According to Emergency Managers, at 2 pm Saturday, approximately 2 inches of snow and ice had accumulated on power lines at the Globe Mobile Home Park. The weight of the heavy snow and ice caused power poles to fall over...and a shelter was then opened.

A cold Pacific low pressure system moved slowly across Arizona on Saturday, December 4th, and brought wintery weather to the the lower deserts of south central Arizona. Scattered to numerous showers occurred ahead of the main low center, and the cold airmass resulted in significant frozen precipitation, including graupel, small hail and some snow. Numerous trained weather spotters across the greater Phoenix area reported pea sized hail during the afternoon hours. At approximately 750 pm a spotter located at 99th Avenue and Happy Valley road reported pea sized hail up to 2 inches deep. Graupel and small hail were reported at 15th Avenue and Osborne. In addition, at 930 pm a spotter near Lake Pleasant reported 1 to 3 inches of a snow/hail mix at Scorpion Bay. The frozen precipitation made for hazardous driving conditions across the Phoenix metropolitan area during the day on Saturday. Fortunately, no major accidents or injuries were reported due to the dangerous driving conditions.

A cold and wet Pacific low pressure system moved to the east, and into New Mexico, during the morning hours on December 4th. Partial clearing combined with wet grounds allowed areas of dense fog to develop over portions of the south central Deserts. Some of the most dense fog occurred over the east and southeast portions of the greater Phoenix metropolitan area. Numerous trained weather spotters reported dense fog, with visibilities at or below one quarter of a mile. Locations experiencing dense fog included Sun Lakes, Chandler Heights, Gilbert, Paradise Valley and Mesa. A spotter at Ocotillo and Higley roads reported visibility down to 2 car lengths in dense fog at 748 am. Satellite and spotter reports also indicated that dense fog was present from the Gila Bend area east to Casa Grande.

The second in a series of cold Pacific low pressure systems moved into central Arizona from the northwest on Monday December 5th. The system prompted the issuance of a winter storm warning above 3500 feet for southern Gila county during the daytime hours on Monday. According to a report from a Co-op observer, 4 inches of snow was observed in Globe as of 10 am. The snow level over south central Arizona lowered to near 2000 feet during the day, and light accumulations were observed across the foothills of the lower deserts, mainly north and east of greater Phoenix, in locations such as north Scottsdale, Carefree and Cave Creek. The Old Real Market building in Miami suffered roof damage caused by heavy snow, as awnings at the top of the building broke off and fell to the ground.

A wet and slow moving Pacific low pressure system brought widespread showers, some with locally heavy rain, to the central Arizona deserts on December 13th. Rainfall continued through the morning hours on December 14th, and many lower desert locations recorded more than one inch of rainfall during the event. Local media reported that Hunt Highway, or State Route 87, was closed between Arizona Farms Road and Merrill Ranch Parkway due to surface damage to the road. The road was reported closed at 730 am on December 14th. The damage was due to the excessive rainfall that fell in the area. The location of the closure was south of the San Tan Valley.

Clearing skies and wet ground in the wake of a departing Pacific low pressure system led to the development of widespread dense fog over the western Arizona deserts during the morning hours on December 14th. A number of trained weather spotters reported dense fog with visibility at or below one quarter mile. A spotter one mile west of Tacna reported dense fog with visibility down to 100 yards at 954 am. Dense fog was also reported by the Parker Sheriff's Office; they indicated that dense fog in Vicksburg Junction lowered visibility below 10 feet at 330 am. Fortunately, no significant accidents or injuries were reported due to the low visibilities and potentially dangerous driving conditions.

Generally clear skies, light wind and lingering low level moisture allowed locally dense fog to form over portions of the lower central and southwestern Arizona desert during the morning hours on December 15th. At 725 am, a trained weather spotter reported dense fog with a visibility down to one quarter mile at the intersection of Gilbert Road and the Hunt Highway, about 5 miles east of Sun Lakes. Another weather spotter in Queen Creek near the San Tan Mountain reported visibility down to 100 feet at 810 am. The fog disrupted the morning rush hour across the greater Phoenix area, and hindered travel along other major Arizona roads including Interstate 10 and Highway 60. Fortunately no significant accidents or injuries were reported with the hazardous driving conditions.

An elderly couple, Mr and Mrs Davis, left Globe on Thursday December 1st with the intent to drive northeast on US 60 to Socorro, New Mexico. They accidentally missed their turn and headed east on Highway 70. After realizing the mistake they attempted to rejoin US 60 by taking a remote forest road that appeared to reconnect with the highway. The road, most likely Indian Road 10 out of San Carlos, was remote and rocky. About 10 miles north on this road, and in very isolated high country, the vehicle became disabled after the transmission hit some rocks and broke.  The couple attempted to wait in the car for help, and unfortunately a pair of cold and wet winter storms moved into southern Gila county and trapped them in their car. The storms brought locally heavy snow and very cold temperatures. Mr and Mrs Davis survived in the vehicle for 5 days with no food and water. While gas remained in the car, they periodically turned it off and on to generate heat. The vehicle ran out of gas on Tuesday December 6th and since the storms had passed the couple decided to try and reach the highway on foot. Detectives indicated that Elizabeth Davis only made it a few hundred feet before she collapsed and died. Mr Davis tried to revive his wife, then continued walking. He was eventually found by an officer from the Arizona Game and Fish Department near US 60 just before noon on December 6th. He was dehydrated, disoriented, but alive.

A cold and wet Pacific low pressure system moved across Arizona on Thursday, December 22nd and it brought winter weather conditions to the higher terrain of southern Gila county. A winter weather advisory was issued for the evening hours, and was cancelled shortly after midnight. Snow and sleet were reported in the area around Roosevelt between 530 and 615 pm. By 730 pm, one half inch of new snow was reported in the Globe area by a trained weather spotter. The snow and sleet led to slippery and dangerous driving conditions; at 730 pm the Globe Sheriff's office reported that highway 60 was closed north of Globe at MP 255 due to snow accumulation. At 810 pm, they also reported multiple 911 calls about accidents on US 60 near Top-of-the-World near MP 238. DPS closed the highway in that area due to dangerous driving conditions. Fortunately, no serious injuries were reported.

Strong, gusty north to northwest winds developed across eastern Riverside county during the morning hours on January 8th. The atmosphere was very dry and the gusty winds, in excess of 35 mph, led to development of dust storm conditions over portions of the county. At noon, fire department and rescue personnel reported dust and sand reducing visibility along Interstate 10 7 miles west of Blythe. Poor visibility was reported westward to Desert Center. In addition, a trained weather spotter reported visibility below one quarter mile 25 miles west of Blythe on Interstate 10, with similar conditions occuring west through Desert Center. Fortunately, no accidents or injuries were reported due to the dense blowing dust and sand.

A cold and wet Pacific low pressure system moved slowly east across Arizona on February 14th, and it brought scattered to numerous rain showers to the central deserts as well as locally heavy snow to the higher elevations east of Phoenix. At 210 pm, a trained weather spotter in Globe reported 3 inches of heavy wet snowfall just north of Globe. Area roads such as U.S. 60 and State Route 77 were reported to be slick.

A powerful, cold and wet Pacific low pressure system moved into southeast California during the afternoon hours on February 15th, bringing widespread rain showers to Joshua Tree National Park. The rain turned to snow by late evening, and locally heavy snow was observed across the park into the morning hours on February 16th. According to the Joshua Tree NP park ranger, 8 to 10 inches of wet snow fell overnight above 4000 feet. Snow covered many of the park roads and fell all the way to the Lost Horse valley floor. By 6 am Thursday, 8 inches of new snow was estimated 9 miles east-northeast of Lost Horse at Keys View.

A cold and wet Pacific low pressure system brought rain and snow showers to southern Gila county, beginning shortly after midnight. Snow levels lowered to below 4000 feet by early morning and slick roads developed in the area around Globe and Miami. Heavy snow was not reported, but the amounts were sufficient to cause hazardous driving conditions. According to law enforcement personnel, at around 5 am a car accident occurred on Highway 77 south of Globe, due to the slick road conditions. Snow amounts at the time were less than one inch. No injuries were reported.

A cold and wet Pacific upper low moved into Arizona on March 18th, and the air mass became rather unstable. Isolated thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening hours, and some of them produced strong gusty winds. At 714 pm, the official weather station at Phoenix Sky Harbor airport recorded a peak wind gust of 59 mph. No damage was reported at the airport due to the strong winds.

A strong, cold and wet Pacific low pressure system moved into Arizona during the day on Sunday, March 18. The system brought widespread showers of rain and snow to the higher terrain east of Phoenix. Snow levels fell to near 3000 feet overnight Sunday night into Monday morning. A number of trained weather spotters across southern Gila County reported locally heavy snow which began Sunday morning and continued into Monday morning. One weather spotter in Globe at 4600 foot elevation reported a minimum of 5 inches new snow as of 8 AM Monday morning. Several additional reports of 2 inches or more in the Globe-Miami area were received. Conditions at Top of the World were bad enough to close US 60, and conditions were equally as poor on highway 60/77 heading towards Show Low. As of 1030 pm on the 18th, law enforcement and rescue personnel had been dispatched to many accidents. There was a serious accident on highway 77 towards Show Low, but crews were having a difficult time getting through due to snowpacked conditions.

events.cz_name: IMPERIAL COUNTY EXCEPT THE LOWER COLORADO RIVER VALLEY
events.event_narrative: A Pacific low pressure system brought windy conditions to Imperial county early on the 3rd of March. The official weather station at El Centro reported a measured west wind gust to 50 knots at 0735Z or 35 minutes past midnight. The high gust resulted in a squall being reported in the special surface observation. No damages were reported with the strong wind gust.

An upper level low pressure system moved south and into southwest Arizona during the afternoon and evening on May 7th, and some mid level moisture moved in with the upper low. The atmosphere became unstable, and virga showers developed in the Yuma area shortly after midnight. Strong and gusty winds developed in the vicinity of the virga, estimated to be in excess of 50 knots. According to the Yuma Police, at 140 AM on the 8th, 14 power poles were downed at County 14th Street and Avenue 2E in the Tierra Mesa subdivision. In addition, fence and barn roof damage was reported near County 16th Street and Avenue A. There was no indication of thunderstorms in the Yuma area overnight, and no lightning was observed. However, the atmospheric conditions allowed the gusty winds to take on the characteristics of a damaging microburst.

A low pressure system moving east across southern Arizona spread moisture into south central Arizona which led to scattered thunderstorms over the lower deserts during the afternoon hours on May 9th. According to a trained weather spotter, microburst wind gusts estimated at 70 knots damaged 8 mobile homes in the Pleasant Valley Mobile Home Park at approximately 435 PM. The park was located near Germain and Ironwood, about 5 miles east of Queen Creek. Six of the homes had their northeast-facing awnings removed. The strong winds lifted up the overhangs and in some cases removed portions of the roofs. Many of these homes were blown off of their foundations. The strong microburst winds were likely enhanced by a gustnado, which increased the severity of the damage. In addition to the mobile home damage, the strong winds blew down a number of power lines in the area.

An upper level low pressure system moving east across southern Arizona spread moisture into eastern Arizona and led to scattered thunderstorms across the central deserts during the afternoon hours on May 9th. A few storms generated gusty and damaging winds estimated to be in excess of 60 knots. At 439 PM, a trained weather spotter reported that small trees and large limbs were down over the road at Ray and Cooper in Gilbert. Another weather spotter in Chandler reported that three large trees, all of them 36 inches wide, were blown over near south Dobson road and East Market Place at approximately 5 PM. Pictures of the downed trees were taken and sent to the Phoenix WCM.

An upper level low pressure system moving eastward across southern Arizona spread moisture into eastern Arizona and scattered thunderstorms developed over the central deserts during the afternoon hours on May 9th. A few of the storms generated strong, damaging microburst winds. At 5 PM, a 58 MPH wind gust was measured four miles north of the town of Maricopa. The wind gust was reported by an official COOP weather observer.

An upper level low pressure system moving east across Arizona spread moisture into south central Arizona, and led to the development of scattered afternoon thunderstorms on May 9th. Some of the storms produced locally heavy rainfall, in addition to strong and damaging microburst winds. At 515 PM, a trained weather spotter in east Mesa reported localized street flooding on Broadway road between Sossamon and 80th Street. A nearby Guadalupe Channel ALERT site measured 0.91 inches of rainfall. The street flooding created hazardous driving conditions during the late afternoon rush hour.

An upper level low moving east across southern Arizona spread moisture into south central Arizona and led to scattered thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours on May 9th. Some of the storms in the Gila Bend area produced damaging microburst winds with peak gusts estimated to be at least 60 knots. As reported by the local utility company, at approximately 615 PM the gusty winds downed a tree which blocked traffic on Pima Road and Highway 85. Construction debris from Interstate 8 and Bypass 85 was strewn about by the strong winds. In addition, power lines were downed by sustained winds reported to be in excess of 45 mph and this left most of the town of Gila Bend without power.

An upper level low pressure system moving east across southern Arizona spread moisture into eastern Arizona and led to the development of scattered thunderstorms over the central deserts during the afternoon hours on May 9th. The storms generated gusty microburst winds in excess of 60 knots, and the outflow winds moving over dry ground produced a series of dust storms. Beginning at around 4 PM, several trained spotters in the Coolidge and Casa Grande areas reported visibilities at or below one quarter mile in dense blowing dust. Spotters indicated that wind gusts were 35 to 40 mph or greater as the dust storm moved through the area. The dense blowing dust created very hazardous driving conditions during the afternoon rush hour, however no significant accidents were reported.

An upper level low pressure system moving east across southern Arizona spread moisture into eastern Arizona and led to the development of scattered thunderstorms over the central deserts during the afternoon hours on May 9th. The storms generated gusty microburst winds in excess of 60 knots, and the outflow winds moving over dry ground produced a series of dust storms; one of these affected the greater Phoenix metropolitan area. At 427 PM, a trained spotter four miles south of Gilbert reported a dust storm. The dense blowing dust primarily affected the southern and southeast portions of the greater Phoenix area. The dense blowing dust created hazardous driving conditions during the afternoon rush hour, fortunately no significant accidents were reported.

An upper level low pressure system moving east across southern Arizona spread moisture into eastern Arizona and led to the development of scattered thunderstorms over the central deserts during the afternoon hours on May 9th. The storms generated gusty microburst winds in excess of 60 knots, and the outflow winds moving over dry ground produced a series of dust storms. One of the dust storms moved into southwest Maricopa county late in the afternoon and impacted the community of Gila Bend. At 616 PM, the official weather station at the Gila Bend airport measured a peak wind gust to 49 knots and reported zero mile visibility in a dust storm.

Southeast flow ahead of a vigorous upper level low pressure system spread moisture into south central Arizona on May 9th. This led to the development of scattered thunderstorms over the central deserts during the afternoon and early evening hours. A few storms in the greater Phoenix area produced damaging microburst winds, estimated to be 50 knots or higher. According to SRP, a local utility company, the winds downed 9 12-kilovolt poles, most of them in north-central Phoenix. Over 4800 people were without power at the peak of the storms.

A Pacific low pressure system and associated cold front moved to the northeast and across the central Arizona deserts during the day on May 26th. The frontal passage produced occasional strong and gusty winds, with peak gusts estimated to be in excess of 35 mph. According to the Arizona Republic, at 1045 in the morning, a wind gust estimated to be around 40 mph caused a 500 pound fence to topple over. The fence, which moved back and forth on a wheel, apparently gave way in a strong wind gust and fell on a 2 year boy, causing his death. The fence struck the young boy in the head.

According to the Santa Rosa @ SR 84 Maricopa County Flood Control District gage, 1.54 inches of rainfall were observed a in 3 hour period ending at 11:30 AM on the 4th of July. Similar values were observed at a nearby gage to the east, Santa Cruz @ SR 84. Both gages were located along State Route 84, between the communities of Stanfield and Casa Grande. The heavy rainfall caused the Santa Rosa wash to run heavily. Water ponding on State Route 84 caused the temporary closure of the road during the late morning and early afternoon hours. No accidents were reported on SR 84. The heavy rain was produced by a cluster of thunderstorms that developed ahead of a weather disturbance approaching from northwest Mexico.

A cluster of thunderstorms developed in the area from Casa Grande southeast to Arizona City; the storms produced locally heavy rainfall during the late morning hours on July 4th. Radar estimates, as well as surrounding rain gage reports, suggested that three hourly totals between one and two inches occurred in the community of Arizona City between 9 am and noon. A weather report received via CoCoRaHS indicated 1.05 inches of rain fell in Arizona City, as of 9 am. Pinal county law enforcement reported road closures in Arizona City due to heavy rainfall. According to a local news report, a number of residents of Arizona City experienced significant urban flooding during the morning due to the heavy rains; water up to a foot deep flooded their subdivisions and flowed into their homes, causing water damage to the first floor as well as their patios/pavers. Insufficent drainage allowed the locally heavy rains to quickly pond up across the lower elevations of Arizona City, and the water levels remained high through the afternoon hours.

Scattered to numerous showers, and isolated thunderstorms, developed across south central Arizona during the morning hours on July 4th, and they produced locally heavy rain which affected the communities of Casa Grande and Maricopa. Based on radar estimates and surrounding rain gage reports, rainfall in excess of one inch fell within a 3 hour period ending by 11:30 am.  At 9:30 am, the Casa Grande Fire Department/Rescue reported local street flooding in Casa Grande with water 3-4 inches deep over area roads. Local media reported road closures from Murphy Road to White and Parker Road along the West Maricopa-Casa Grande Highway southeast of Maricopa, due to the locally heavy rainfall.

Strong thunderstorms developed over southeastern Arizona during the middle of the afternoon on June 16th, and they produced gusty outflow winds as high as 45 mph. The winds pushed to the northeast, picking up substantial amounts of dust and dirt and a dust storm was generated. At 435 a trained spotter in Coolidge reported visibility below one quarter mile in blowing dust. At 503 pm, another trained weather spotter in Casa Grande reported a haboob approaching from the southeast. Visibility dropped to less than 1/8 of a mile in dense blowing dust.

Strong thunderstorms developed across southeastern Arizona during the middle of the afternoon on June 16th, and they produced gusty outflow winds as high as 45 mph. The winds spread to the northwest and produced a dust storm; at approximately 5 pm a spotter in Casa Grande reported a haboob approaching from the southeast. The haboob then moved into the southeast portion of the greater Phoenix area during the late afternoon hours. At 520 pm a trained spotter at Gilbert and Riggs road reported visibility below 1/8 of a mile in dense blowing dust. The dust then moved into the west valley; at about 7 pm weather spotters in Suprise and north Glendale reported blowing dust with visibilities below 1/4 of a mile. The dense blowing dust produced hazardous driving conditions to motorists across the greater Phoenix area, fortunately no major accidents were reported.

Intense thunderstorms developed across southeast Arizona during the afternoon hours on June 27th. The storms generated strong and gusty outflow winds which spread into portions of northern Pinal county. According to law enforcement personnel, at about 615 pm microburst wind gusts estimated to be near 70 knots overturned a double wide trailer in the community of Toltec. The strong winds also blew down a number of power poles in the area.

Strong thunderstorms developed over southeastern Arizona during the afternoon hours on June 27th. Gusty outflow winds in excess of 40 mph spread to the northwest across portions of northern Pinal county and generated dust storm conditions. At 626 pm, a trained spotter in Coolidge reported visibility below 1/4 mile in dense blowing dust. Another spotter in the San Tan Valley, near Combs & Schnepf Farms roads, reported a dust storm at 7 pm. The spotter estimated gusts to 45 mph which lowered visibility to 1/4 mile in blowing dust.

Strong thunderstorms developed across southeastern Arizona during the afternoon hours on June 27th. Gusty outflow winds in excess of 45 mph spread to the northwest and into the greater Phoenix area during the evening hours, producing dust storm conditions. At about 8 pm, a trained spotter in central Phoenix reported visibility down to 200 feet at US Airways Center. At 740 pm, another spotter in Ahwatukee reported a dust storm with visibility less than 1/4 mile at 42nd & Frye. In addition, the KIWA AWOS automatic weather station indicated 1/4 mile visibility and 46 mph wind gusts shortly after 7 pm. The dense blowing dust produced very hazardous driving conditions across the greater Phoenix area, especially during the latter portions of the rush hour.

Scattered showers and thunderstorms containing locally heavy rainfall developed across south central Arizona during the morning hours on July 4th, and they affected the greater Phoenix area. A trained weather spotter in Surprise, near the intersection of Greenway and Reems roads, indicated that approximately 1.5 inches of rain fell between 1115 am and 1230 pm. Nearly three quarters of an inch fell in 45 minutes, and the heavy rain flooded their yard.

Strong high pressure aloft over the desert southwest led to excessive heat across the southwestern Arizona deserts on July 11th. An excessive heat warning had been in effect since 2 pm Monday, and remained in effect through 8 pm Wednesday. Although high temperatures lowered to around 110 on Wednesday, highs across the western Arizona and southeast California deserts reached between 115 and 118 on the 9th and 10th. Despite the excessive heat warning the heat proved deadly for a Somerton man on July 11th. According to an article in the Yuma Sun, shortly after 8 pm, firefighters were dispatched to a residence in the 3300 block of West Mandarina Street. When the firefighters entered the home, they realized there was no air conditioning and temperatures were in excess of 100 degrees. They found a 72 year old man in his bedroom, unconcious and unresponsive. They removed him from the home and treated him in their ambulance before transferring him to the Yuma Regional Medical Center. Despite the medical care, he passed away. Earlier in the day, at 1130 am, firefighters treated a 37 year old man working outside at the West Cocopah Reservation. The man was experiencing a heat emergency, and was having seizures. He was transported to YRMC and survived.

Isolated thunderstorms developed during the evening hours across the central Arizona deserts. Some of the storms produced gusty and damaging outflow winds. At 945 pm, a trained weather spotter 5 miles northeast of Glendale reported a tree blown down at 52nd Avenue and Thunderbird road. The wind gusts were estimated to be around 50 knots.

Thunderstorms, which developed over the south central Arizona deserts during the evening hours on July 11th, persisted into the early morning hours on July 12th. Although most of the storms produced locally heavy rainfall, a few managed to generate gusty and damaging outflow winds. According to local broadcast media, shortly after midnight wind gusts estimated at 60 knots blew down a billboard at 24th Street and University. A few large trees were also uprooted. The damage occurred about 2 miles west of Phoenix Sky Harbor airport.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across Imperial county during the late morning and then continued well into the day on July 13th. The storms generated heavy rain over central portions of the county, including Calipatria, and this led to areal flooding of roads, washes and low lying areas. Between 4 and 5 pm, a cluster of thunderstorms east of Calipatria  produced 2 to 3 inches of rain based on radar estimates, highly increasing the threat of flooding. At approximately 10 pm, Imperial county emergency management personnel reported flooding into agricultural fields between Calipatria and Niland due to overflowing canals. Water was reported to be coming in from the east. Flood waters were affecting 24 homes in the Calipatria area, and there was a report of damage to the Highline Canal. In addition, Blair road at the entrance into the Calipatria State Prison was flooded.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across northwest Imperial county during the early afternoon hours on July 13th. The storms persisted in the area for several hours and produced locally heavy rainfall in the area to the west of Salton Sea. At 427 pm, the California Highway Patrol reported the closure of State Route 78, west of the junction with highway 86, due to flooding. In addition, there were reports of several vehicles trapped in running washes as well as flooding across other area roadways.

A weather disturbance moving into a very moist and unstable atmosphere led to numerous showers and thunderstorms across Imperial county during the afternoon and evening hours on July 13th. Radar indicated that between one and two inches of rain fell across portions of southwest Imperial county from 215 to 315 pm and a flash flood warning was issued for areas including the communities of Seeley and Plaster City. According to California Emergency Managers, at 6 pm there was a water rescue of an irrigation district employee at the intersection of Drew Road and the railroad tracks approximately one mile west of the town of Seeley.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across southern Gila county during the morning hours on July 13th, and they persisted into the afternoon. The storms produced locally heavy rainfall which led to running washes, flooding of area streets and overflowing creeks. At 1128 am, a trained spotter in Globe reported street flooding. At 1240 pm, law enforcement personnel indicated that a creek was overflowing approximately 3 miles southeast of Cutter. No reports of injuries or property damage were received in response to the heavy rains.

Scattered to numerous thunderstorms, many with heavy rain, developed across south central Arizona during the afternoon hours on July 14th. A few of the storms were able to produce moderate to large hail. At 330 pm, a trained weather spotter in Globe reported large hail, measured at three quarters of an inch in diameter. At approximately the same time,  another spotter 2 miles northwest of the Boyce Thompson Arboretum reported hail one quarter of an inch in diameter. No damage was reported due to the large hail.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across La Paz county during the late morning and afternoon hours on July 14th. Due to the very moist and unstable nature of the atmosphere, the many of the storms generated heavy rain which led to episodes of flash flooding. Thunderstorms developed in the area around Quartzsite late in the morning; as of 130 pm radar estimated that 2 to 3 inches of rain had fallen since 1130 am.  According to Arizona Department of Transportation, at 2 pm state highway 95 was closed at mile post 113.5 due to flooding. This location was in the town of Quartzsite.

Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed across portions of La Paz county, starting in the late morning and continuing through the afternoon hours. Due to the very moist and unstable nature of the atmosphere, many storms produced heavy rain which led to episodes of flash flooding. Radar indicated that 2 to 3 inches of rain, or more, had fallen in the area around Quartzside and Brenda beginning late in the morning and continuing into the middle of the afternoon. The rain led to the closure of highway 95 at Quartzsite at about 2 pm. At 430 pm, a trained spotter 1 mile west of Quartzside reported that numerous washes in town were running heavily, and many streets were closed due to high water.

Scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms developed across portions of La Paz county, including the area around Bouse, during the late morning hours and they continued through the afternoon. Due to the very moist and unstable nature of the atmosphere, the storms produced heavy rain which led to episodes of flash flooding. Flash flood warnings were in effect for central La Paz county, including Bouse, beginning at 1238 pm and continued through the afternoon. At 310 pm, a trained weather spotter 1 mile south of Bouse reported that the Bouse wash was running heavily and flooding.

Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed across much of La Paz county, including the area around Bouse, during the late morning hours on July 14th, and they continued through the afternoon hours. Due to the very moist and unstable nature of the atmosphere, the storms produced heavy rain which led to episodes of flash flooding. Flash flood warning were in effect for central La Paz county, including Bouse, from 1238 pm through the late afternoon. At 5 pm, fire department and rescue personnel reported flash flooding along Highway 72, forcing the closure of the road at mile marker 12 due to water flowing across the roadway.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across south central Arizona during the afternoon hours on July 14th, and some of them affected the Wickenburg area. Due to the very moist and unstable  nature of the atmosphere, the storms tended to produce heavy rainfall which led to episodes of flash flooding. A flash flood warning had been issued for the Wickenburg area starting at 503 pm on the 14th. According to a trained weather spotter, at 618 pm the heavy rains led to a mudslide which blocked the westbound lanes of US 60 at mile marker 115.

Numerous thunderstorms developed across the greater Phoenix metropolitan area during the afternoon hours on July 14th. Due to the very wet and unstable nature of the airmass, most of the thunderstorms produced very heavy rain. A few generated wet microbursts with damaging winds. At 345 pm, a Weather Service employee reported that numerous trees had been blown down at the San Tan Village Mall in Gilbert Ranch. One of the trees was about 40 feet tall and it fell over and landed on an automobile, causing significant damage. Peak wind gusts were estimated to be about 65 knots. No injuries were reported.

Widespread thunderstorms developed over the greater Phoenix metropolitan area during the afternoon hours on July 14th. Due to the very moist and unstable nature of the airmass, most of the storms generated very heavy rain. However, isolated storms produced wet microbursts with damaging winds across southeastern portions of the Phoenix area. At 404 pm, a trained weather spotter located in Gilbert reported several trees down along Greenfield road between Ray and Warner roads. The largest trees were around 12 inches in diameter. Peak wind gusts were estimated to be about 65 knots. No injuries were reported due to the fallen trees.

Numerous thunderstorms developed across the greater Phoenix area during the afternoon hours on July 14th, especially across the southeast valley. Due to the very moist and unstable airmass in place, most of the storms generated locally heavy rain, with the highest rain rates observed to be in excess of 2 inches per hour. According to a trained weather spotter in Gilbert, 2.25 inches of rain fell between 330 pm and 430 pm at a home located at Val Vista and Elliot roads. The heavy rain led to some street flooding at the San Tan Village Mall. Marble sized hail also occurred, along with some gusty winds that damaged a few trees in the area.

Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed across the greater Phoenix metropolitan area, especially the southeastern valley communities, during the afternoon hours on July 14th. Due to the very moist and unstable nature of the atmosphere, the storms generated locally heavy rainfall which led to widespread street flooding. According to a trained weather spotter 2 miles southwest of Gilbert, 1.1 inches of rain fell between 330 pm and 4 pm. Several additional weather spotters in the southeast valley, including communities such as Gilbert, Chandler and Seville, reported similar amounts of rainfall between 330 pm and 5 pm. Commonly, the reports indicated that around one inch of rain fell within a 30 minute period. For example, at 442 pm a trained spotter 2 miles west of Apache Junction reported 0.93 inches of rain measured in the past half-hour.

Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed over the greater Phoenix metropolitan area, especially the southeast valley communities, during the afternoon hours on July 14th. Due to the very moist and unstable nature of the atmosphere, the storms generated locally heavy rain which led to flooding and flash flooding across portions of the southeast valley. Heavy rain began by 3 pm or so, and a flash flood warning was issued starting at 343 pm. According to Arizona Department of Transportation (ADOT) personnel, the excessive rain caused four lanes of US 60 - the Superstition Freeway - to be blocked off in each direction, approximately 2 miles south of Mesa. The freeway was blocked by 430 pm and remained closed well into the evening.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across southwestern Maricopa county during the early afternoon hours on July 14th, mainly south and east of Gila Bend. Due to the very moist and unstable nature of the atmosphere, the storms generated locally heavy rainfall which led to some flash flooding. According to Arizona Department of Transportation (ADOT), a flash flood near Mobile resulted in the closure of Highway 238 between mileposts 0 and 38.

Scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms developed across the greater Phoenix metropolitan area during the afternoon hours on July 14th. Due to the very moist and unstable nature of the atmosphere, the storms generated heavy rain which led to episodes of flash flooding. Beginning around 330 pm, flash flooding developed in the southeastern valley communties, including Gilbert and Chander, and flash flood warnings were issued. Heavy rain then developed further to the north and east, and at 5 pm there was a public report of flash flooding in Goldfield Ranch, on the eastern fringe of the Phoenix metropolitan area. A wash along the Beeline Highway was reported to be flowing rapidly, and flooding out of its banks. Fortunately, no injuries were reported due to the flash flooding.

Numerous thunderstorms developed across the greater Phoenix metropolitan area, especially the southeastern valley communities, during the afternoon hours on July 14th. Due to the very moist and unstable nature of the atmosphere, the storms generated intense rainfall which led to episodes of flash flooding. Heavy rain in excess of 2 inches fell in the Gilbert area between 330 pm and 430 pm. During the peak of the heavy rainfall, approximately 1.5 inches of rain fell within 10 minutes, causing the collapse of the roof at Tees and More located at 313 North Gilbert Road. According to the store owners, Pete and Barb Addiego, the roof collapse caused at least 110 thousand dollars in damaged equipment and inventory. Fortunately, no injuries were reported.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across southwestern Yuma county during the evening hours on July 13th. Due to the very moist and unstable nature of the airmass, some storms were able to generate intense rainfall with rainfall rates in excess of 2 inches per hour. At 1015 pm, a trained weather spotter located about one mile west of Yuma International Airport reported a 4 hour rainfall total of 2.4 inches. The same event dropped 1.66 of rain at the official Yuma weather station (Yuma ASOS) and this broke the daily record by almost one inch. The heavy rain led to street flooding and caused area washes to run heavily.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across La Paz county during the early afternoon hours on July 14th. Due to the wet and unstable nature of the airmass, most of the storms produced heavy rain which led to episodes of flash flooding. A few storms managed to produce wet microbursts, leading to gusty and damaging winds. According to APS, an Arizona utility company, gusty winds downed several power poles along Highway 95 north of Quartzsite at about 2 pm. One pole was downed 5 miles to the north, and an additional two were downed 8 miles to the north. Peak wind gusts were estimated to be at least 50 knots.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across southern Gila county during the afternoon hours on July 20th, and the storms produced locally heavy rainfall with rainfall rates in excess of one inch per hour. At 419 pm, a trained weather spotter one mile east of Globe reported 0.87 inches of rainfall with the past 40 minutes. At 349 pm, another weather spotter in Globe reported one half of an inch of rain within 20 minutes, a rainfall rate of 1.5 inches per hour. The heavy rain led to the issuance of an Urban and Small Stream Flood Advisory for southern Gila county, including the Globe area.

Scattered thunderstorms moved through south central Arizona during the afternoon hours on July 21st, and some of them produced gusty and damaging microburst winds. According to a trained weather spotter 6 miles east of the Tonto National Monument, at 415 pm thunderstorm winds estimated at 60 mph uprooted a 20 inch diameter Mulberry tree. In addition, the strong winds tore metal off of a storage shed and ripped some shingles off of a nearby roof.

Scattered thunderstorms developed over the higher terrain of southeast Arizona during the afternoon hours, then moved towards the northwest and into the greater Phoenix area by late afternoon. In addition to generating dense blowing dust, the storms also created strong, gusty and damaging outflow winds. At 5 pm, a trained weather spotter 2 miles west of Apache Junction reported that strong winds had ripped a number of shingles off of his roof. He estimated the wind gusts to be at least 40 mph.

Scattered thunderstorms developed to the southeast of the greater Phoenix area during the afternoon hours on July 21st. The storms produced strong and gusty outflow winds which moved northwest and into the Phoenix metropolitan area during the late afternoon. The winds, which were in excess of 50 mph at times, generated dense blowing dust and dust storm conditions. At 511 pm, a trained weather spotter 2 miles southwest of Firebird Lake, or in far southwest Chandler, measured a wind gust to 63 mph. At the time, a dust storm was in progress with zero visibility in dense blowing dust.

Strong thunderstorms developed over southeast Arizona during the afternoon hours on July 21st, and they generated strong and gusty outflow winds which moved to the northwest and into the greater Phoenix area in the late afternoon. At 555 pm, the KIWA AWOS weather station at Phoenix Mesa-Gateway Airport recorded a measured wind gust to 52 knots.

Scattered strong thunderstorms developed across southeast Arizona during the afternoon hours on July 21st. They generated strong gusty outflow winds in excess of 40 mph which moved into the greater Phoenix area during the late afternoon and produced dense blowing dust. Some of the storms then moved into the southeast portions of the greater Phoenix area and produced strong, damaging microburst winds which enhanced the earlier outflow winds. A trained weather spotter in far East Mesa reported a variety of wind damage at approximately 545 pm. He reported damage to an awning, a carport taken off by wind, windows blown out and cactus trees blown over.

Scattered thunderstorms moved into the greater Phoenix metropolitan area during the evening hours on July 21st. The storms were accompanied by strong gusty outflow winds, and dense blowing dust. Some of the storms generated damaging microburst winds as well. At 710 pm, there was a public report of 2 trees downed by wind about 6 miles east of Peoria. The wind gusts were estimated to be about 60 knots, and the trees were rather large with diameters of 12 inches.

Scattered  thunderstorms developed across southeast Arizona during the afternoon hours on July 21st. The storms produced strong outflow winds in excess of 40 mph which spread northwest across the deserts of northern Pinal county. The gusty winds picked up copious amounts of dust and dirt and generated dust storm conditions. At 4 pm a trained spotter near Arizola reported one eighth of a mile visibility in blowing dust; by 418 pm visibility dropped to zero mile and cars were pulled onto the side of the road. At 428 pm a spotter 7 miles east of Sacaton reported a dust storm with zero visibility and wind gusts to 35 mph. In addition, spotters in communities such as San Tan Valley and Apache Junction reported dust storm conditions with winds gusting as high as 50 mph.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across southeast Arizona during the afternoon hours on July 21st. The storms generated strong outflow winds in excess of 40 mph which spread to the northwest and picked up massive quantities of dust. A dust storm was created which moved into the the southeast portion of the greater Phoenix metropolitan area after 430 pm...and continued to overspread the area through 630 pm. Numerous trained weather spotters reported dust storm conditions with winds gusting in excess of 40 mph, and visibilities below one quarter mile in dense blowing dust. A trained spotter 4 miles west of Apache Junction reported a dust storm at 447 pm, with 40 mph winds and visibility below one eighth of a mile. At 527 pm a storm chaser near Firebird Lake reported a dust storm with periods of visibility down to 100 feet. Another trained spotter near Firebird Lake reported that emergency vehicles had responded to an accident caused by the blowing dust. Finally, at about 5 pm a trained spotter near Seville reported a wind gust to 52 mph along with zero visibility in dense blowing dust.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across southeast Arizona during the afternoon hours on July 21st and they spread northwestward and into the greater Phoenix area during the evening hours. In addition to strong gusty winds and dense blowing dust, some of the storms produced locally heavy rainfall which led to urban flooding.  At 745 pm a trained spotter 6 miles east of Peoria reported heavy rain which caused local washes to run and curb to curb street flooding. In addition, a local retention basin had filled up due to the heavy rainfall.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across southeast Arizona during the afternoon hours on July 21st and they generated strong gusty outflow winds in excess of 40 mph. The winds picked up substantial amounts of dust and sand as they spread west, and created dust storm conditions over the southwest Arizona deserts. At 730 pm a trained weather spotter in Dateland reported a dust storm, with visibility down to one eighth of a mile in dense blowing dust. A dust storm warning was issued shortly afterwards for the southwest Arizona deserts. No accidents or injuries were reported due to the dense blowing dust.

Scattered thunderstorms developed to the south and southwest of the greater Phoenix area during the afternoon hours on July 23rd. The storms produced gusty outflow winds in excess of 30 mph which moved north and picked up copious amounts of dust. A dust storm was generated which moved into the greater Phoenix area and primarily affected the central and western valley communities. At 405 pm, a trained spotter reported visibility below 100 yards in a dust storm at 51st Avenue and Dobbins. At 438 pm a trained spotter in downtown Phoenix at 7th Street and Jefferson reported near zero visibility in dense blowing dust. Additionally, at 445 pm another spotter near Papago Park reported visibility below one quarter mile in blowing dust at 52nd Street and McDowell Road. The reports helped trigger a dust storm warning for the greater Phoenix area. The dense blowing dust created very hazardous driving conditions during the evening rush hour. Fortunately, no significant accidents or injuries were reported.

Thunderstorms developed across south central Arizona during the afternoon and early evening hours on July 23rd. In addition to producing dense blowing dust in the greater Phoenix area, some of the storms generated strong wind gusts in excess of 50 mph. At 630 pm, a trained spotter near Queen Valley reported a thunderstorm wind gust estimated to be 60 mph. No damage occurred as a result of the strong gust.

Scattered thunderstorms developed across northeast Maricopa county during the afternoon hours on July 28th, and some of them produced locally heavy rainfall. At about 4 pm, the upper Sycamore Creek Canyon precipitation gage on the upper portion of the burn reported 0.87 inches of rain within a 15 minute period. This amount of rain, coupled with additional rainfall, led to flash flooding along Sycamore Creek as well as the burn area and the community of Sunflower. At 551 pm, DPS reported that Sycamore wash was flooding with water reaching homes in Sunflower. At 556 pm, a report from ArizonaNewsnet indicated a flood approaching the Sycamore Creek Beeline Highway bridge at milepost 212. Additional reports near 6 pm indicated water was out of the banks of Sycamore creek and covering area roads in and around Sunflower.

Thunderstorms developed during the afternoon hours on July 29th and they affected portions of the greater Phoenix area, including the community of Fountain Hills. Some of the thunderstorms produced damaging microburst wind gusts estimated to be at least 65 knots. According to local broadcast media reports, at approximately 230 pm, the strong winds uprooted trees in Fountain Hills and also damaged roof tiles on some homes.

Thunderstorms developed over the greater Phoenix area during the afternoon hours on July 29th, and some of the storms generated gusty and damaging microburst winds. According to a trained weather spotter 5 miles northeast of San Tan Valley, at 355 pm gusty winds estimated to be at least 60 knots blew down a number of trees.
